units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Integers: below zero
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 Mathematics, Term 3: Integers (count, order and compare integers; add and subtract integers; integers in context)
units.intention: Today I am working with numbers below zero.
units.prompt: How did the number line help you?

lesson.say: Integers are whole numbers, including negative numbers. Negative numbers are less than zero. Minus five degrees is colder than zero degrees.
lesson.html:
−3→−2→−1→0→1→2→3

Numbers to the left of 0 are negative. The further left, the smaller.

lesson.say: Minus eight is less than minus two, because it is further left on the number line.
lesson.html:
−8→<→−2

Think of temperature: −8 °C is colder than −2 °C.

lesson.say: Adding a positive number moves right. Subtracting moves left. Minus three plus five equals two. Two minus six equals minus four.
lesson.html:
−3 + 5 = 2→2 − 6 = −4

Subtracting a negative is the same as adding: 4 − (−3) = 4 + 3 = 7.

example.q: At 6 am it was −4 °C in Sutherland. By noon it was 9 degrees warmer. What was the temperature at noon?
steps: Warmer means add.
Start at −4 and move 9 to the right.

questions.q: Which is the smallest?
hints: Negative numbers are left of zero.
questions.explain: −7 is the smallest.

questions.q: What is −6 + 10?
hints: You pass 0 after 6 steps, then 4 more.

questions.q: What is 3 − 8?
hints: 3 steps gets you to 0, then 5 more.

questions.q: What is 5 − (−2)?
Order from smallest to biggest.
A diver is 12 m below sea level and swims up 5 m. Where is she now?
questions.explain: −12 + 5 = −7, so 7 m below sea level.

units.parent: Your child compared, added and subtracted negative and positive numbers.
units.teacher: Shows ordering integers and adding and subtracting integers, including subtracting a negative, in context.
units.done: Negative numbers are less than zero. Use a number line to add and subtract.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Squares, cubes and roots
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 Mathematics, Term 1: Exponents (squares, cubes, square roots and cube roots; exponential form)
units.intention: Today I am using exponents to write repeated multiplication.
units.prompt: How is squaring different from doubling?

lesson.say: Two to the power of four means two times two times two times two, which is sixteen. The small number is the exponent.
lesson.html:
2⁴→=→2 × 2 × 2 × 2→=→16

The base is 2. The exponent 4 says how many times to multiply it.

lesson.say: Five squared is five times five, which is twenty-five. Three cubed is three times three times three, which is twenty-seven.
lesson.html:
5² = 25→3³ = 27

🟩 🧊

Squared makes the area of a square. Cubed makes the volume of a cube.

lesson.say: The square root of forty-nine is seven, because seven squared is forty-nine. The cube root of eight is two, because two cubed is eight.
lesson.html:
√49 = 7→∛8 = 2

A root works backwards.

example.q: A square garden has an area of 64 m². How long is each side?
steps: Area of a square = side × side.
Which number times itself is 64?
8 × 8 = 64, so each side is 8 m.

questions.q: What is 6 squared?
What is 4 cubed?
What is the square root of 81?
Which is the same as 10 × 10 × 10?
Which is bigger, 2⁵ or 5²?
questions.explain: 2⁵ = 32 is bigger than 5² = 25.

units.parent: Your child worked with squares, cubes, square roots and cube roots.
units.teacher: Shows exponential notation, calculating squares and cubes, and finding square and cube roots.
units.done: An exponent tells you how many times to multiply. Roots work backwards.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Solving simple equations
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 Mathematics, Term 3: Algebraic equations (write equations from descriptions; solve by inspection and by trial and improvement)
units.intention: Today I am finding the missing number in an equation.
units.prompt: How did you check your answer?

lesson.say: An equation says two things are equal. x plus four equals ten. The letter x stands for a number we do not know yet.
lesson.html:
x + 4→=→10

An equation is balanced, like a scale.

lesson.say: To solve x plus four equals ten, undo adding four by subtracting four. Ten minus four is six, so x is six.
lesson.html:
x + 4 = 10→x = 10 − 4→x = 6

Use the opposite operation to find x.

lesson.say: Put your answer back in. Six plus four equals ten. It works.
lesson.html:
6 + 4 = 10→✓

Substitute your answer to check it.

example.q: Solve 3x = 21.
steps: 3x means 3 times x.
Undo times 3 by dividing by 3: 21 ÷ 3.

questions.q: Solve: x + 9 = 15
Solve: 4y = 32
Solve: m − 7 = 12
Thabo thinks of a number, doubles it and adds 3. He gets 17. Which equation fits?
Solve: 2n + 3 = 17

units.parent: Your child solved simple equations by undoing operations and checking the answer.
units.teacher: Shows writing and solving one- and two-step linear equations by inverse operations and substitution.
units.done: Undo each operation to find the unknown, then check.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Short story: The Last Bus
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 English Home Language: Reading and Viewing (short story: plot, conflict, character, setting; inference)
units.intention: Today I am reading a short story and analysing its plot and conflict.
units.prompt: What would you have done in Kaya's place?
units.passage:
The Last Bus (a 2to.iQ short story)

Kaya checked her phone again. 17:52. The last bus to Mdantsane left at six, and she was still three blocks from the rank.

She had stayed late to finish the science project, because her partner, Ludwe, had not shown up. Again.

She ran. Her school bag bounced against her back like a drum. At the corner, an old man was struggling to lift a crate of oranges onto his cart. Kaya slowed down. If she stopped, she would miss the bus. If she didn't, he might hurt himself.

She stopped. Together they lifted the crate. "Enkosi, ntombi," he said, and pressed two oranges into her hands.

When she reached the rank, the bus was pulling away. Kaya's heart sank. Then she saw Ludwe at the back window, waving wildly at the driver. The bus stopped.

"I'm sorry about today," Ludwe said as she sat down, breathing hard. Kaya handed him an orange. "Tomorrow," she said, "you're doing the poster."

lesson.say: Read the story, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
The Last Bus (a 2to.iQ short story)

Kaya checked her phone again. 17:52. The last bus to Mdantsane left at six, and she was still three blocks from the rank.

She had stayed late to finish the science project, because her partner, Ludwe, had not shown up. Again.

She ran. Her school bag bounced against her back like a drum. At the corner, an old man was struggling to lift a crate of oranges onto his cart. Kaya slowed down. If she stopped, she would miss the bus. If she didn't, he might hurt himself.

She stopped. Together they lifted the crate. "Enkosi, ntombi," he said, and pressed two oranges into her hands.

When she reached the rank, the bus was pulling away. Kaya's heart sank. Then she saw Ludwe at the back window, waving wildly at the driver. The bus stopped.

"I'm sorry about today," Ludwe said as she sat down, breathing hard. Kaya handed him an orange. "Tomorrow," she said, "you're doing the poster."

lesson.say: Conflict is the problem in a story. Kaya faces an inner conflict: help the old man, or catch the bus.
lesson.html:
Kaya→vs→time

Inner conflict is a struggle inside a character's mind. Outer conflict is with another person or with the world.

lesson.say: The climax is the moment of greatest tension, when the bus pulls away. We learn about characters from what they do. Kaya stops to help, so she is kind.
lesson.html:
Setting→Rising action→Climax→Resolution

Show, don't tell: actions reveal character.

example.q: What does Kaya's choice to stop tell us about her?
steps: She knew she might miss the bus.
She still chose to help a stranger.
She is kind and puts others first.

questions.q: Where is the story set?
options: On the way to a bus rank
hints: She needs to catch a bus.
questions.explain: Kaya is rushing through town to the bus rank.

questions.q: What is Kaya's inner conflict?
options: Whether to help the man or catch the bus
hints: It is a choice in her mind.
Two things she wants pull against each other.
The bus or the old man.
questions.explain: She must choose between helping and catching the bus.

questions.q: Her school bag bounced against her back like a drum. What is this?
questions.explain: It compares using like, so it is a simile.

questions.q: Why does Ludwe stop the bus?
options: He feels sorry for letting her down
hints: What does he say to Kaya?
He wants to make up for it.
questions.explain: He apologises, so he is trying to make up for not helping with the project.

questions.q: Put the plot in order.
items: Kaya is late because she worked alone
She stops to help the old man
questions.explain: Late, helps the man, the bus leaves, Ludwe stops it.

reflect.q: How did you understand the story best?

units.parent: Your child read a short story and analysed its conflict, plot and characters.
units.teacher: Shows identifying setting, inner conflict, plot structure, a simile and inferring character motivation.
units.done: Stories are driven by conflict, and actions reveal character.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Figures of speech
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 English Home Language: Language Structures and Conventions; Literature (figurative language: simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole, alliteration)
units.intention: Today I am identifying figures of speech and their effect.
units.prompt: Which figure of speech do you use when you talk?

lesson.say: A simile compares using like or as. He ran like the wind. A metaphor says one thing is another. The classroom was a zoo.
lesson.html:
Simile: like / as→Metaphor: is

Both compare. A metaphor is stronger because it says the thing is the other.

lesson.say: Personification gives human actions to things that are not human. The wind whispered through the trees.
lesson.html:
The wind whispered through the trees.

Wind cannot whisper. It is given a human action.

lesson.say: Hyperbole is huge exaggeration. I have told you a million times. Alliteration repeats the first sound. Seven slippery snakes.
lesson.html:
Hyperbole: a million times→Alliteration: seven slippery snakes

Writers use these for effect: to make us feel, see or remember.

example.q: What figure of speech is: My bag weighs a ton?
steps: Does the bag really weigh a ton?
No, it is a huge exaggeration.
It is hyperbole.

questions.q: Her smile was as bright as the sun. What is this?
questions.explain: It compares using as, so it is a simile.

questions.q: The old car groaned up the hill. What is this?
questions.explain: A car is given a human action: personification.

questions.q: Time is a thief. What is this?
hints: No. Time is said to be a thief.
questions.explain: It says time is a thief, so it is a metaphor.

questions.q: Big brown bears bounce. What is this?
questions.explain: The repeated b sound is alliteration.

questions.q: What is the effect of: I'm so hungry I could eat a horse?
options: It shows how very hungry the speaker is
It tells us the speaker likes horses
hints: Is it meant to be true?
questions.explain: The hyperbole emphasises extreme hunger.

reflect.q: Which figure of speech is easiest to spot?

units.parent: Your child identified similes, metaphors, personification, hyperbole and alliteration.
units.teacher: Shows identifying figures of speech and explaining their effect.
units.done: Figures of speech help writers create pictures and feelings.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Direct and reported speech
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 English Home Language: Language Structures and Conventions (direct and indirect speech; tense changes; punctuation)
units.intention: Today I am changing direct speech into reported speech.
units.prompt: What changes when you report what someone said?

lesson.say: Direct speech gives the exact words, inside speech marks. Sipho said, I am tired.
lesson.html:
Sipho said, "I am tired."

Direct: the exact words in inverted commas.

lesson.say: Reported speech tells what someone said without their exact words. Sipho said that he was tired.
lesson.html:
Sipho said that he was tired.

Reported (indirect): no speech marks, often with that.

lesson.say: In reported speech, the tense moves back. Am becomes was. Will becomes would. I becomes he or she. Today becomes that day.
lesson.html:
am → was→will → would→I → he/she→today → that day→here → there

Pronouns, tenses and time words shift.

example.q: Change to reported speech: Lindi said, "I will call you tomorrow."
steps: Remove the speech marks and add that.
I becomes she. Will becomes would. You becomes me or the listener.
Lindi said that she would call me the next day.

questions.q: Which is reported speech?
options: Ama said that she was hungry.
hints: Reported speech has no speech marks.
questions.explain: Ama said that she was hungry. is reported speech.

questions.q: Neo said, "I am playing soccer." Report it.
options: Neo said that he was playing soccer.
Neo said that I am playing soccer.
Neo said he is play soccer.
Neo said that he will play soccer.
hints: Am playing moves back to was playing.
Neo said that he was playing soccer.
questions.explain: I → he, am → was.

questions.q: In reported speech, will usually becomes …
questions.explain: Will becomes would.

questions.q: Mom said, "Come here." Which is correct reported speech?
options: Mom told me to come there.
Mom told me that come here.
hints: A command becomes told someone to.
Mom told me to come there.
questions.explain: Commands are reported with told … to, and here becomes there.

questions.q: Which word often joins the reporting verb to the reported words?
questions.explain: He said that he was tired.

units.parent: Your child practised changing direct speech into reported speech.
units.teacher: Shows conversion from direct to indirect speech, including tense, pronoun and time-word changes and reported commands.
units.done: Reported speech shifts the tense, pronouns and time words.

units.subject: Natural Sciences
units.title: Biodiversity and classification
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 Natural Sciences, Life and Living: Biodiversity (classification of living things; vertebrates and invertebrates; plants with and without seeds; importance of biodiversity)
units.intention: Today I am classifying living things into groups.
units.prompt: Why do scientists classify living things?

lesson.say: Biodiversity is the variety of all living things in an area. South Africa has some of the highest biodiversity in the world.
lesson.html:
🦏 🌿 🐋 🦋 🌸

Bio means life. Diversity means variety.

lesson.say: Animals with a backbone are vertebrates: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Animals without a backbone are invertebrates, such as insects, spiders and worms.
lesson.html:
Fish→Amphibians→Reptiles→Birds→Mammals

Vertebrates have a backbone. Invertebrates do not.

lesson.say: Every species plays a role. Bees pollinate crops. Wetlands clean water. When we lose species, ecosystems become weaker.
lesson.html:
🐝 → 🍎

Biodiversity gives us food, medicine and clean water.

example.q: A gecko has dry, scaly skin, lays eggs on land and has a backbone. Which group is it in?
steps: It has a backbone, so it is a vertebrate.
Dry, scaly skin and eggs on land.
It is a reptile.

questions.q: Which animal is an invertebrate?
hints: Frogs, eagles and sharks have backbones.
questions.explain: A spider has no backbone.

questions.q: Which group has hair or fur and feeds its young on milk?
hints: Think of a dog or a human.
questions.explain: Mammals have hair and feed young on milk.

questions.q: A frog lives in water as a tadpole and on land as an adult. Which group?
hints: It lives two lives: water and land.
questions.explain: Frogs are amphibians.

questions.q: Vertebrate or invertebrate?
questions.explain: Snail and earthworm are invertebrates. Penguin and lizard are vertebrates.

questions.q: Why is biodiversity important?
options: Ecosystems need many species to stay healthy
questions.explain: Many species working together keep ecosystems healthy.

options: Asking: does it have a backbone?

units.parent: Your child learned about biodiversity and classified animals into vertebrate and invertebrate groups.
units.teacher: Shows classification of animals by key features and explaining the importance of biodiversity.
units.done: Scientists group living things by their features.

units.subject: Natural Sciences
units.title: Separating mixtures
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 Natural Sciences, Matter and Materials: Separating mixtures (hand sorting, sieving, filtration, decanting, evaporation, distillation, chromatography)
units.intention: Today I am choosing the right method to separate a mixture.
units.prompt: Which method would you use at home?

lesson.say: A sieve separates big pieces from small ones. A filter lets liquid through and traps solid particles, like sand in muddy water.
lesson.html:
🥣 ☕

Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid.

lesson.say: When salt is dissolved in water, filtering will not work. Heat the solution. The water evaporates and the salt is left behind.
lesson.html:
Salt water→Heat→Salt crystals

Evaporation gets back a dissolved solid.

lesson.say: Distillation boils a liquid and cools the steam to collect pure water. Chromatography separates the colours in ink as water moves up paper.
lesson.html:
Boil→Steam→Cool→Pure water

🖊️ 📄 🌈

Each method uses a different property.

example.q: How would you separate sand, salt and water?
steps: First filter: the sand stays in the filter paper.
The salt water passes through.
Then evaporate the water to get the salt.

questions.q: Which method separates sand from water?
questions.explain: Filtration traps the sand.

questions.q: How do you get salt back from salt water?
hints: A filter will not trap it.
questions.explain: Evaporate the water and the salt is left.

questions.q: Which method separates the colours in black ink?
questions.explain: Chromatography separates ink colours.

questions.q: Which method gives you pure drinking water from sea water?
hints: Cool the steam back to liquid.
questions.explain: Distillation collects pure water from steam.

questions.q: Put the steps for separating sand, salt and water in order.
hints: Then deal with the dissolved salt.
questions.explain: Filter, collect, evaporate, salt remains.

reflect.q: What helped you choose a method?

units.parent: Your child learned how to separate mixtures by filtering, evaporating, distilling and chromatography.
units.teacher: Shows selecting separation methods based on properties such as solubility and particle size.
units.done: Choose a separation method based on the properties of the mixture.

units.subject: Natural Sciences
units.title: How heat moves
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 Natural Sciences, Energy and Change: Heat transfer (conduction, convection, radiation; insulation and energy saving)
units.intention: Today I am learning the three ways heat moves.
units.prompt: Where do you see heat moving at home?

lesson.say: Conduction is heat moving through a solid, by touch. A metal spoon in hot tea gets hot all the way up.
lesson.html:
🥄 ☕

Metals are good conductors. Wood and plastic are insulators.

lesson.say: Convection is heat moving through liquids and gases. Warm water or air rises, cool water or air sinks, making a current.
lesson.html:
Warm rises→Cool sinks→Current

Convection currents heat a pot of water.

lesson.say: Radiation is heat moving as invisible waves, even through empty space. The sun warms Earth by radiation.
lesson.html:
☀️ 〰️ 🌍

Radiation needs no particles. Dark, dull surfaces absorb it best.

example.q: Why do pots have plastic or wooden handles?
steps: Metal conducts heat well.
Plastic and wood are insulators.
The handle stays cool, so you do not get burnt.

questions.q: How does heat travel through a metal rod?
questions.explain: Heat moves through solids by conduction.

questions.q: How does a heater warm a whole room?
questions.explain: Warm air rises and circulates by convection.

questions.q: How does heat from the sun reach Earth?
hints: No particles to pass it on.
questions.explain: Radiation can travel through empty space.

questions.q: Which is the best insulator?
questions.explain: Wool traps air and is a good insulator.

questions.q: Why do people in hot places often paint roofs white?
questions.explain: White reflects the sun's radiation and keeps the house cooler.

reflect.q: Which way of heat moving made most sense?

units.parent: Your child learned how heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing the three modes of heat transfer and applying insulation to everyday contexts.
units.done: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Self-image and peer pressure
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 Life Orientation: Development of the self in society (self-image; peer pressure; personal strengths; respect for self and others)
units.intention: Today I am thinking about how I see myself and how to handle peer pressure.
units.prompt: What is one thing you like about yourself?

lesson.say: Self-image is how you see yourself. It is shaped by your family, friends, media and your own thoughts. A healthy self-image accepts strengths and things you are working on.
lesson.html:
🪞

Social media shows edited lives. Compare yourself to who you were yesterday, not to a filter.

lesson.say: Peer pressure is when people your age push you to do something. It can be positive, like studying together, or negative, like skipping class.
lesson.html:
Positive: join a team→Negative: bunk school

Peer pressure can go either way.

lesson.say: To resist negative pressure: say no clearly, give a reason or suggest something else, and walk away if you need to. Choose friends who respect your no.
lesson.html:
Say no→Give a reason→Suggest something else→Walk away

Being assertive is clear and respectful.

example.q: Friends dare Lebo to share a rude photo of a classmate. What can she do?
steps: It would hurt the classmate and could be against school rules or the law.
She says: No, that's not cool.
She suggests something else, and tells an adult if the photo is being shared.

questions.q: Which is positive peer pressure?
options: Friends encourage you to join the choir
Friends tell you to skip school
hints: Which one is good for you?
questions.explain: Being encouraged to join the choir is positive.

questions.q: Which is an assertive response?
options: Doing it so they like you
questions.explain: A clear, calm no is assertive.

questions.q: What shapes your self-image?
hints: Family, friends, media and our thoughts.
questions.explain: Family, friends, media and our own thoughts all shape self-image.

questions.q: Why can comparing yourself to social media be unhelpful?
options: Posts are often edited and show only the best moments
hints: Do people post their bad days?
questions.explain: Social media often shows edited highlights, not real life.

questions.q: Sort the strategies.
items: Keep it secret when someone is in danger
hints: Which ones keep you true to yourself?
Giving in and hiding danger do not help.
Walking away and suggesting something else help.
questions.explain: Walking away and suggesting something else are helpful.

units.parent: Your child explored self-image and practised assertive ways to handle peer pressure.
units.teacher: Shows understanding of influences on self-image, positive and negative peer pressure, and assertive refusal skills.
units.done: You can say no clearly and respectfully.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Rights and responsibilities
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 Life Orientation: Constitutional rights and responsibilities (the Bill of Rights; children's rights; responsibilities that go with rights)
units.intention: Today I am learning about my rights and the responsibilities that go with them.
units.prompt: Which right matters most to you, and why?

lesson.say: South Africa's Constitution was adopted in 1996. Chapter 2 is the Bill of Rights. It protects the rights of everyone in the country.
lesson.html:
📜 ⚖️

The Constitution is the highest law in South Africa.

lesson.say: Everyone has the right to equality, dignity, life, freedom of expression and a basic education. Children have extra protection, such as the right to be protected from abuse and harmful work.
lesson.html:
Equality→Dignity→Education→Freedom of expression

Section 28 protects children's rights.

lesson.say: If you have the right to education, you have the responsibility to attend and let others learn. Your freedom of expression must not be used to spread hate.
lesson.html:
Right to education→→→Respect others' learning

My rights end where they harm someone else's.

example.q: You have freedom of expression. Can you post lies about a classmate?
steps: Freedom of expression is a right.
But your classmate has a right to dignity.
No. Rights have limits and come with responsibilities.

questions.q: Which chapter of the Constitution is the Bill of Rights?
hints: It comes early in the Constitution.
questions.explain: The Bill of Rights is Chapter 2.

questions.q: Which responsibility goes with the right to education?
options: Attend school and respect others' learning
questions.explain: Attending and respecting others' learning goes with the right to education.

questions.q: Which right protects people from unfair discrimination?
hints: No one is less than another.
questions.explain: The right to equality protects against unfair discrimination.

questions.q: In what year was the current Constitution adopted?
hints: Two years after the first democratic election.
questions.explain: The Constitution was adopted in 1996.

questions.q: Right or responsibility?
hints: A right is something you are entitled to.
A responsibility is something you must do.
Not bullying and caring for property are duties.
questions.explain: Safety and education are rights. Not bullying and caring for property are responsibilities.

reflect.q: Which right matters most to you?

units.parent: Your child learned about the Bill of Rights and the responsibilities that go with rights.
units.teacher: Shows knowledge of the Bill of Rights, children's rights and linking rights to responsibilities.
units.done: Every right comes with a responsibility.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Study skills that work
units.caps: CAPS Grade 7 Life Orientation: World of work (study skills and study methods; planning a study timetable; learning styles and strategies)
units.intention: Today I am learning study methods that help me remember.
units.prompt: Which study method will you try this week?

lesson.say: Re-reading feels easy but does not help much. Testing yourself, by covering your notes and trying to recall, helps you remember far better.
lesson.html:
Read→Cover→Recall→Check

Active recall beats re-reading.

lesson.say: Study a little each day instead of everything the night before. Short sessions spread over time help memory.
lesson.html:
Mon→Wed→Fri→Sun

Spaced practice: 25 minutes, then a 5-minute break.

lesson.say: Mind maps, flow diagrams and summaries in your own words help you see how ideas connect.
lesson.html:
🧠 🗺️

Turn notes into pictures, diagrams or questions.

example.q: Zinhle has a science test on Friday. It is Monday. How should she plan?
steps: Split the work into small parts.
Study one part each day, and test herself on earlier parts.
On Thursday, do practice questions, then sleep well.

questions.q: Which method helps memory most?
hints: Which one makes your brain work hardest?
questions.explain: Active recall by testing yourself works best.

questions.q: When is the best time to start studying for a test?
options: A few days before, a little each day
questions.explain: Spaced practice over several days works better than cramming.

questions.q: What is a mind map?
options: A diagram linking ideas to a main topic
hints: The main idea is in the middle.
questions.explain: A mind map links ideas around a central topic.

questions.q: Which is the best study space?
questions.explain: A quiet space without phone distractions helps focus.

questions.q: Put the active recall steps in order.
items: Recall it aloud or on paper
questions.explain: Read, cover, recall, check.

units.parent: Your child learned study methods such as testing yourself, spacing practice and mind maps.
units.teacher: Shows knowledge of evidence-based study strategies and planning study time.
units.done: Test yourself, spread study out, and make it visual.

units.subject: Life and work skills
units.title: Taking a taxi safely
units.caps: CAPS for Learners with Severe Intellectual Disability (draft): Life and work skills (independence: travelling safely by minibus taxi)
units.intention: Today I am learning to take a taxi safely.
units.prompt: Where would you like to travel on your own?

lesson.say: Know where you are going. Have the right money ready. Tell someone at home where you are going.
lesson.html: Know the place→Money ready→Tell someone

lesson.say: Pass your money to the front. Tell the driver where you want to get off. Keep your bag on your lap.
lesson.html: When you want to get off, say: Short left, please.

lesson.say: Sit near other people. If you feel unsafe, get off at a busy place and phone someone you trust.
lesson.html: Feel unsafe? Get off somewhere busy and phone home.

example.q: You want to get off at the next corner. What do you say?
steps: The driver needs to know.
Use the taxi words.
Say: Short left, please.

questions.q: What should you have ready before the taxi comes?
questions.explain: Have the right money ready to pay.

questions.q: How do you tell the driver you want to get off?
questions.explain: Say 'Short left, please' before your stop.

questions.q: You feel unsafe in a taxi. What do you do?
options: Get off at a busy place and phone someone
questions.explain: Get off safely where there are people, and phone someone you trust.

questions.q: Put the trip in order.
items: Tell someone where you are going
questions.explain: Tell someone, get money ready, pay, then say 'Short left'.

units.parent: Your child practised planning and taking a taxi safely.
units.teacher: Shows planning a journey, using taxi etiquette and applying personal safety strategies (independence and community access).
units.done: Plan, have money ready, say 'Short left', and stay safe.

units.subject: Life and work skills
units.title: Shopping with R50
units.caps: CAPS for Learners with Severe Intellectual Disability (draft): Life and work skills (functional numeracy: shopping within a budget and checking change)
units.intention: Today I am shopping with a budget.
units.prompt: What do you buy at the shop most often?

lesson.say: Before shopping, write or draw a list of what you need.
lesson.html:
🍞 🥛 🍌

bread · milk · bananas

lesson.say: Look at the price of each thing. Add them up. Make sure the total is not more than your money.
lesson.html: Bread R18 + milk R20 = R38

lesson.say: If you pay with R50 and spend R38, you get R12 change. Count your change before you leave.
lesson.html: R50 − R38 = R12 change

example.q: You have R50. Bread is R18 and milk is R20. Can you buy both?
steps: R38 is less than R50.
Yes. You get R12 change.

questions.q: Bread costs R18 and milk costs R20. What is the total, in rand?
You have R50. Can you buy things that cost R38 in total?
hints: Is R38 more or less than R50?
questions.explain: R38 is less than R50, so yes.

questions.q: You pay R50 for things that cost R38. How much change do you get, in rand?
What should you do before you leave the till?
questions.explain: Count your change to check it is right.

units.parent: Your child practised shopping with R50: adding prices and checking change.
units.teacher: Shows planning purchases, adding prices, staying within a budget and checking change (functional numeracy: money).
units.done: Make a list, add the prices, and check your change.

units.subject: Life and work skills
units.title: Following instructions at work
units.caps: CAPS for Learners with Severe Intellectual Disability (draft): Life and work skills (work readiness: following multi-step instructions)
units.intention: Today I am learning to follow instructions at work.
units.prompt: What is hard about following instructions?

lesson.say: At work, your supervisor gives instructions. Look at them, listen to all the words, and wait until they finish.
lesson.html: Look→Listen→Wait

lesson.say: Do the steps in order. If there are many steps, ask for them one at a time, or ask for a picture list.
lesson.html: Ask: Can you show me, please?

lesson.say: If you are not sure, ask. It is good to ask. When you finish, say: I am done. What next?
lesson.html: Say: I am done. What next?

example.q: Your supervisor says: 'Fold the towels, then put them on the shelf.' What do you do first?
steps: There are two steps.
The first step is to fold the towels.
Fold the towels first, then put them on the shelf.

questions.q: Your supervisor is talking. What do you do?
questions.explain: Look at your supervisor and listen to every word.

questions.q: You do not understand the instruction. What do you do?
questions.explain: Ask, so you do the job right.

questions.q: 'Sweep the floor, then empty the bin, then wash your hands.' Put the steps in order.
questions.explain: Sweep, empty the bin, wash your hands.

questions.q: You have finished your task. What do you say?
questions.explain: Tell your supervisor and ask what is next.

options: Doing one step at a time

units.parent: Your child practised listening to and following instructions at work.
units.teacher: Shows attending to, sequencing and clarifying multi-step workplace instructions (work readiness).
units.done: Look, listen, do it in order, and ask when you're not sure.

units.subject: Life and work skills
units.title: Greeting customers
units.caps: CAPS for Learners with Severe Intellectual Disability (draft): Life and work skills (work readiness: communicating politely with customers)
units.intention: Today I am learning to greet and help customers.
units.prompt: How do you like to be greeted in a shop?

lesson.say: When a customer comes in, look at them, smile and greet them. Say: Good morning, how can I help you?
lesson.html: Good morning, how can I help you?

lesson.say: Use please and thank you. Speak clearly, not too loud and not too soft.
lesson.html: Please→Thank you→Clear voice

lesson.say: If you don't know the answer, say: Let me call someone to help you. Then find your supervisor.
lesson.html: Let me call someone to help you.

example.q: A customer asks where the bread is, but you don't know. What do you say?
steps: You don't know the answer.
Don't guess or ignore them.
Say: Let me call someone to help you.

questions.q: A customer walks in. What do you do first?
questions.explain: Smile and greet the customer.

questions.q: Which greeting is best at nine o'clock in the morning?
options: 'Good morning, how can I help you?'
questions.explain: 'Good morning, how can I help you?' is polite and right for the time.

questions.q: You can't answer a customer's question. What do you say?
options: 'Let me call someone to help you.'
questions.explain: Politely get someone who can help.

questions.q: A customer says thank you. What do you say?
questions.explain: Say 'You're welcome.'

units.parent: Your child practised greeting and helping customers politely.
units.teacher: Shows using polite greetings, appropriate volume and help-seeking scripts in customer service (work readiness: communication).
units.done: Smile, greet, be polite, and call someone if you can't help.

units.subject: Life and work skills
units.title: Safety signs at work
units.caps: CAPS for Learners with Severe Intellectual Disability (draft): Life and work skills (work readiness: safety signs, protective clothing and reporting hazards)
units.intention: Today I am learning to stay safe at work.
units.prompt: What safety signs have you seen?

lesson.say: At work, signs use colours. Red means stop or fire. Yellow means be careful. Green means safe, like the way out. Blue means you must do something, like wear gloves.
lesson.html: 🔴 stop or fire→🟡 be careful→🟢 safe→🔵 must do

lesson.say: Some jobs need gloves, a mask or safety shoes. They protect your body. Always wear them when the sign says so.
lesson.html:
🧤 😷 🥾

gloves · mask · safety shoes

lesson.say: If you see a spill, a fire or someone hurt, do not try to fix it alone. Tell your supervisor straight away.
lesson.html: Tell your supervisor straight away.

example.q: You see a blue sign with gloves on it. What does it mean?
steps: Blue signs tell you what you must do.
The picture shows gloves.
You must wear gloves here.

questions.q: Which colour means safe, like the way out?
questions.explain: Green means safe.

questions.q: A sign shows a mask. What must you do?
hints: The sign shows what to wear.
questions.explain: Wear a mask where the sign says so.

questions.q: You see water spilled on the floor. What do you do?
questions.explain: Tell your supervisor so nobody slips.

questions.q: What does a yellow sign usually mean?
questions.explain: Yellow signs warn you to be careful.

units.parent: Your child learnt safety sign colours and what to do if something goes wrong at work.
units.teacher: Shows interpreting safety sign colours and symbols, using protective equipment and reporting hazards (work readiness: health and safety).
units.done: Know the colours, wear your protection, and report problems.

units.subject: Life and work skills
units.title: Cleaning a workspace
units.caps: CAPS for Learners with Severe Intellectual Disability (draft): Life and work skills (work readiness: following a cleaning routine safely)
units.intention: Today I am learning to clean a workspace in the right order.
units.prompt: What jobs do you do at home?

lesson.say: Before cleaning, put on gloves and get your cloth, spray and bin bag.
lesson.html: Gloves→Cloth→Spray→Bin bag

lesson.say: Clean from the top to the bottom, so dirt falls down to the floor. Wipe the tables before you sweep the floor.
lesson.html: Shelves→Tables→Floor

lesson.say: Put rubbish in the bin, put the cleaning things away, take off your gloves, and wash your hands.
lesson.html: Rubbish in the bin→Pack away→Wash hands

example.q: Should you sweep the floor before or after wiping the table?
steps: Crumbs from the table fall on the floor.
If you sweep first, the floor gets dirty again.
Wipe the table first, then sweep.

questions.q: Put the cleaning steps in order.
questions.explain: Gloves, table, floor, wash hands.

questions.q: What do you put on before using cleaning spray?
questions.explain: Gloves protect your hands from the spray.

questions.q: Why do we clean from top to bottom?
options: Dirt falls down, so we clean the floor last
questions.explain: Dirt falls, so the floor is cleaned last.

units.parent: Your child learnt a cleaning routine done safely and in the right order.
units.teacher: Shows sequencing a cleaning routine, using protective equipment and applying top-to-bottom logic (work readiness: practical skills).
units.done: Gloves on, top to bottom, pack away and wash your hands.

units.subject: Life and work skills
units.title: Asking for help
units.caps: CAPS for Learners with Severe Intellectual Disability (draft): Life and work skills (self-advocacy: asking for help at work and at home)
units.intention: Today I am learning how to ask for help.
units.prompt: Who do you ask when you need help?

lesson.say: Asking for help is a strength. Workers ask for help every day.
lesson.html: Asking for help is smart.

lesson.say: At work, ask your supervisor or a colleague you trust. At home, ask a family member.
lesson.html: Supervisor→Colleague→Family

lesson.say: Say what you need clearly: Excuse me, can you help me, please? I don't know how to do this.
lesson.html: Excuse me, can you help me, please?

example.q: The printer is jammed and you don't know how to fix it. What do you do?
steps: You don't know how to fix it.
Don't force it or leave it.
Say: Excuse me, can you help me with the printer, please?

questions.q: You are stuck on a task. What do you do?
questions.explain: Ask for help.

questions.q: Who can you ask for help at work?
questions.explain: Ask your supervisor or a colleague.

questions.q: Which is the best way to ask?
options: 'Excuse me, can you help me, please?'
questions.explain: A polite, clear question works best.

units.parent: Your child practised asking for help clearly and politely.
units.teacher: Shows recognising when help is needed, identifying appropriate people and using a polite help-seeking script (self-advocacy).
units.done: It is smart to ask: 'Excuse me, can you help me, please?'

units.subject: Life and work skills
units.title: Being on time
units.caps: CAPS for Learners with Severe Intellectual Disability (draft): Life and work skills (work readiness: reading digital time and planning to arrive on time)
units.intention: Today I am learning to plan so I arrive on time.
units.prompt: What makes it hard to be on time?

lesson.say: At work, you must arrive on time. If you are late, other people have to wait.
lesson.html: Work starts at 8:00.

lesson.say: On a digital clock, the first number is the hour. 7:30 means half past seven.
lesson.html: 7:00 seven o'clock→7:30 half past seven→8:00 eight o'clock

lesson.say: Find out how long the trip takes, then leave early. If the trip takes 30 minutes and work starts at 8:00, leave by 7:30 or a bit earlier. If you will be late, phone your supervisor.
lesson.html:
Start 8:00 − trip 30 minutes = leave by 7:30

Running late? Phone your supervisor.

example.q: Work starts at 9:00. The taxi takes 30 minutes. When should you leave?
steps: Work starts at 9:00.
The trip takes 30 minutes.
Leave by 8:30, or a bit earlier to be safe.

questions.q: What time does 7:30 show?
hints: The first number is the hour: 7.
questions.explain: 7:30 is half past seven.

questions.q: Work starts at 8:00. The trip takes 30 minutes. When should you leave?
questions.explain: 30 minutes before 8:00 is 7:30.

questions.q: The taxi is late and you will be late for work. What do you do?
questions.explain: Phone your supervisor to tell them.

units.parent: Your child practised reading the time and planning to arrive at work on time.
units.teacher: Shows reading digital time, calculating departure times and communicating lateness (work readiness: time management).
units.done: Know the start time, leave early, and phone if you'll be late.

words: a whole number that can be positive, negative or zero
the small number that says how many times to multiply
the number that was multiplied by itself
a statement that two things are equal
a letter that stands for an unknown number
put a number in place of the letter
the main problem in a story
a comparison using like or as
the exact words someone said, in speech marks
telling what someone said without their exact words
the variety of living things in an area
separating a solid from a liquid with a filter
a liquid turning into a gas
boiling a liquid and cooling the steam to collect it
heat moving through liquids and gases in currents
a material that slows heat down
a push from people your age
the highest law of the country
the part of the Constitution that protects everyone's rights
being treated with respect as a person
testing yourself to bring information back from memory
studying a little at a time over several days
